misconceptions.statement: You should drink only when you feel thirsty and never before.
misconceptions.why: Students hear that thirst is the body's alarm, so they trust it fully.
misconceptions.fix: During hard exercise or heat, thirst may lag behind fluid loss, so sip water regularly. In normal rest, thirst is a fine guide.

probe.question: A footballer plays for 90 minutes in the sun. When should she drink?
probe.wrong_answer: Only when she feels very thirsty.

misconceptions.root_belief: one simple rule works in every situation

misconceptions.statement: If you feel thirsty, you are already badly dehydrated and in danger.
misconceptions.why: Sports advertisements say thirst means it is too late.
misconceptions.fix: Thirst starts with a small fluid loss and is a normal signal to drink. It does not mean serious danger.

probe.question: Riya feels thirsty after a short walk. Is she in danger?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, she is already seriously dehydrated.

misconceptions.root_belief: a warning signal means the worst has happened

misconceptions.statement: Everyone needs exactly eight glasses of water every day.
misconceptions.why: The eight glasses rule is repeated everywhere as a fixed number.
misconceptions.fix: Water need depends on age, body size, weather and activity. Eight glasses is only a rough guide.

probe.question: A farmer works in 40 C heat and a child sits in an AC room. How much water does each need?
probe.wrong_answer: Both need exactly eight glasses.

misconceptions.root_belief: one fixed number applies to everyone

misconceptions.statement: Only drinking plain water counts towards the body's water needs.
misconceptions.why: Students link water intake only with a glass of water.
misconceptions.fix: Milk, dal, fruits, vegetables, buttermilk and other drinks also supply water.

probe.question: Does eating watermelon or drinking nimbu pani give the body water?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only plain water does.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the obvious form of a thing counts

misconceptions.statement: You cannot drink too much water, so more is always better.
misconceptions.why: Water is seen as purely healthy and harmless.
misconceptions.fix: Drinking far too much plain water in a short time dilutes blood salts and can make a person ill. Drink to need.

probe.question: A runner drinks 6 litres in an hour. Is that safe because it is only water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, water can never harm.

misconceptions.root_belief: more of a good thing is always better
misconceptions.source_hint: health education studies and sports medicine guidance on exercise-associated hyponatremia

misconceptions.statement: Sports drinks and energy drinks are needed for every sportsperson to stay hydrated.
misconceptions.why: Advertisements show athletes with branded drinks.
misconceptions.fix: Plain water is enough for most school sport. Sports drinks may help only in very long, intense exercise.

probe.question: A student plays 30 minutes of cricket in the playground. What should she drink?
probe.wrong_answer: A sports drink, since water is not enough.

misconceptions.root_belief: advertised products are necessary

misconceptions.statement: Cold fizzy drinks hydrate you best on a hot day.
misconceptions.why: Cold sweet drinks feel refreshing so students think they work better.
misconceptions.fix: Sugary fizzy drinks are not the best for hydration. Water, lemon water or buttermilk is better.

probe.question: After playing in heat, which drink is best for rehydration: cola or water?
probe.wrong_answer: Cola, because it is cold and refreshing.

misconceptions.root_belief: what feels good must work best

misconceptions.statement: Drinking cold water in summer is harmful and only warm water hydrates.
misconceptions.why: Family advice about cold water causing colds is generalised.
misconceptions.fix: Water at any temperature hydrates the body equally. Cool water may even be easier to drink in heat.

probe.question: Does ice-cold water hydrate less than lukewarm water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, only warm water hydrates properly.

misconceptions.root_belief: temperature changes what a substance fundamentally does

misconceptions.statement: If you are not sweating, you are not losing any water.
misconceptions.why: Students only notice water loss when sweat is visible.
misconceptions.fix: The body also loses water through breathing, urine and invisible sweat, even in cool weather.

probe.question: Aman sits in a cool room and does not sweat. Is he losing water?
probe.wrong_answer: No, no sweat means no water loss.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's ideas about the human body and excretion

misconceptions.statement: Sweat cools you because the liquid itself is cold.
misconceptions.why: Wet skin feels cool, so students think sweat is cold.
misconceptions.fix: Sweat cools the body when it evaporates and takes heat from the skin.

probe.question: Why does sweating cool the body?
probe.wrong_answer: Because sweat is a cold liquid.

misconceptions.root_belief: a thing cools because it is itself cold
misconceptions.source_hint: concept research on evaporation and cooling in school science

misconceptions.statement: Sweating more always cools you more, even on a very humid day.
misconceptions.why: Students think more sweat always means more cooling.
misconceptions.fix: Only evaporated sweat cools you. In humid air, sweat evaporates slowly and drips off, so cooling is poor.

probe.question: On a humid coastal day you are dripping with sweat. Are you cooling well?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more sweat means more cooling.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Sweat is pure water, so only water needs replacing after heavy sweating.
misconceptions.why: Sweat looks like clear water.
misconceptions.fix: Sweat contains salts such as sodium. After heavy or long sweating, salts are also lost.

probe.question: What is lost in sweat besides water?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, sweat is only water.

misconceptions.root_belief: clear liquids are pure substances

misconceptions.statement: Clear, pale urine shows dehydration, and dark urine shows you are well hydrated.
misconceptions.why: Students link a darker colour with being stronger or healthier.
misconceptions.fix: Pale yellow urine usually means good hydration. Dark yellow urine often means the body needs more water.

probe.question: Your urine is dark yellow. What does it suggest?
probe.wrong_answer: That you are well hydrated.

misconceptions.root_belief: a stronger colour means a better state

misconceptions.statement: Dehydration only happens in hot weather.
misconceptions.why: Dehydration is taught together with summer and sweating.
misconceptions.fix: Dehydration can happen in cold weather, in illness with vomiting or diarrhoea, or at high altitude.

probe.question: A child has diarrhoea in winter. Can he be dehydrated?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is not hot.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Dehydration is dangerous only for adults who play sports.
misconceptions.why: Hydration advice is usually shown with athletes.
misconceptions.fix: Babies, young children and elderly people can become dehydrated quickly, especially in diarrhoea or heat.

probe.question: Who is most at risk from diarrhoea-related dehydration, a baby or an athlete?
probe.wrong_answer: The athlete, because sportspeople lose more water.

misconceptions.root_belief: a risk applies only to the commonly shown group

misconceptions.statement: ORS is just sugar water, and more sugar makes it work better.
misconceptions.why: Students see the sweet taste and think sugar is the active part.
misconceptions.fix: ORS has salts and a small amount of glucose in the right balance. Extra sugar can worsen diarrhoea.

probe.question: A mother adds 4 spoons of sugar to ORS to make it stronger. Is this good?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more sugar makes it work better.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: public health guidance and studies on home-prepared ORS errors

misconceptions.statement: Packet ORS can be mixed with any amount of water, and the amount does not matter.
misconceptions.why: Students think a solution works the same whatever its concentration.
misconceptions.fix: ORS must be mixed with the exact amount of clean water printed on the packet. Too little or too much water changes how well it works.

probe.question: A packet says mix in 1 litre. A child mixes it in a small glass. Is that fine?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the amount of water does not matter.

misconceptions.root_belief: concentration does not matter, only the ingredients

misconceptions.statement: ORS is only for people with serious sickness in hospital, not for use at home.
misconceptions.why: Medicines are usually linked with doctors and hospitals.
misconceptions.fix: ORS is safe to give at home at the first sign of diarrhoea or dehydration. Seek a doctor if the person is very weak or not improving.

probe.question: A child has loose motions at home. Should the mother wait for the hospital before giving ORS?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, ORS is only given in hospital.

misconceptions.root_belief: treatment belongs only to experts

misconceptions.statement: During diarrhoea a person should stop drinking fluids to stop the loose motions.
misconceptions.why: Students think less intake means less output.
misconceptions.fix: Fluid loss in diarrhoea must be replaced, so give ORS and other fluids more often.

probe.question: A child has diarrhoea. Should we stop giving water and ORS?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, stop drinking so that it stops.

misconceptions.root_belief: remove the input to stop the output

misconceptions.statement: Heatstroke is the same as ordinary tiredness from heat and goes away with rest.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up heat exhaustion, tiredness and heatstroke.
misconceptions.fix: Heatstroke is an emergency with very high body temperature and confusion. It needs urgent cooling and medical help.

probe.question: A man in the sun is confused, very hot and has stopped sweating. What should be done?
probe.wrong_answer: Let him rest a while, it is only tiredness.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding things are the same

misconceptions.statement: A person with heatstroke will always be sweating a lot.
misconceptions.why: Students link heat illness with sweating.
misconceptions.fix: In some heatstroke cases, the skin is hot and dry because the body's cooling has failed. Sweating or not, high temperature and confusion are the key signs.

probe.question: A hot, dry-skinned person is confused. Can it be heatstroke since he is not sweating?
probe.wrong_answer: No, heatstroke always has heavy sweating.

misconceptions.root_belief: a typical sign is always present

misconceptions.statement: For a person with heatstroke, give a very large amount of water at once and keep them wrapped warmly.
misconceptions.why: Students link care for illness with warmth and drinking plenty.
misconceptions.fix: Move the person to shade, cool the body with water or wet cloth, give sips only if awake, and call for medical help.

probe.question: What is the first step for a person with heatstroke?
probe.wrong_answer: Cover them with a blanket and make them drink a lot.

misconceptions.root_belief: the same care suits every illness

misconceptions.statement: Hard exercise in the afternoon sun is fine if you drink water.
misconceptions.why: Students think water alone fully protects them from heat.
misconceptions.fix: Water helps, but exercise in peak afternoon heat still risks heat illness. Choose cooler hours and take breaks.

probe.question: Is it safe to run a 10 km race at 2 pm in May if you carry water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, water makes it completely safe.

misconceptions.root_belief: one precaution removes the whole risk

misconceptions.statement: Tea, coffee or alcohol are good ways to rehydrate in summer.
misconceptions.why: They are liquids, so students think all liquids hydrate equally.
misconceptions.fix: Alcohol dehydrates, and too much caffeine may increase urine. Water and ORS are the best choices.

probe.question: After a hot match, which is better to drink: water or strong coffee?
probe.wrong_answer: Strong coffee, since all liquids hydrate equally.

misconceptions.root_belief: things in the same category behave the same

misconceptions.statement: ORS is only needed for children and is useless for adults.
misconceptions.why: ORS packets are mostly shown with babies in health posters.
misconceptions.fix: ORS helps people of all ages who lose fluids and salts through diarrhoea, vomiting or heavy sweating.

probe.question: An adult has vomiting and loose motions. Will ORS help?
probe.wrong_answer: No, ORS is only for children.

misconceptions.root_belief: a risk applies only to the commonly shown group

misconceptions.statement: Wiping off sweat quickly with a towel cools you down better than letting it dry.
misconceptions.why: Students think removing sweat removes heat directly.
misconceptions.fix: Cooling happens as sweat evaporates from the skin. Wiping it off removes the water without using its cooling effect.

probe.question: Is it better to let sweat evaporate or wipe it away to cool down?
probe.wrong_answer: Wiping it away cools you better.

misconceptions.root_belief: removing the visible thing fixes the problem
